|**20. Do the clinical trials on the technology reflect**<br>**current UK clinical practice?**<br>•<br>If not, how could the results be extrapolated to the UK<br>setting?<br>•<br>What, in your view, are the most important outcomes,<br>and were they measured in the trials?<br>•<br>If surrogate outcome measures were used, do they<br>adequately predict long-term clinical outcomes?<br>•<br>Are there any adverse effects that were not apparent in<br>clinical trials but have come to light subsequently?|Yes, the PROTECT trial reflects current practice in the UK (134 patients were<br>randomised from Europe). The demographic of patients (70% male, 67% whilte,<br>28% Asian, 1% Black) is also representative of the UK population with IgAN.<br>The key outcome for IgAN is rate of change of eGFR, and this was measured in<br>the trial.<br>Change in proteinuria was the primary endpoint in the pre-specified interim<br>analysis. This does accurately predict outcome in patients with IgAN.<br>To my knowledge, there are no adverse effects that were not apparent in clinical<br>trials that have come to light subsequently.|
|**21. Are you aware of any relevant evidence that might**<br>**not be found by a systematic review of the trial**<br>**evidence?**|An open label trial is exploring the use of sparsentan as first line treatment in<br>patients with proteinuric IgAN. Results have been published in abstract form and<br>presented at the ISN 2024: WCN24-773 SPARSENTAN AS FIRST-LINE<br>TREATMENT OF INCIDENT PATIENTS WITH IgA NEPHROPATHY:<br>PRELIMINARY FINDINGS FROM THE SPARTAN TRIAL-Kidney International<br>Reports<br>In this small study, proteinuria reduced by 80% after 36 weeks of treatment and<br>67% patients achieved complete proteinuric remission (<0.3 g/day) during follow|

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

Most patients with IgAN progress to kidney failure within 15–20 years of diagnosis, and the mean age at kidney failure or death is 

48 years. 

There are very few treatments currently available for IgAN 

Sparsentan has been shown in a multi-national RCT to reduce proteinuria and slow progression of IgAN, and as such should delay the need for renal replacement therapy, which is costly both for the NHS and for patients. 

It is a safe and well tolerated drug that can easily be introduced into clinical practice 

As it is likely to be an expensive treatment, I recommend that treatment decision to start treatment with sparsentan should be made as part of an MDT, attended by more than one nephrologist with experience of treating IgAN, to ensure it is used appropriately. 

Thank you for your time.

What is your experience of living with primary IgA**<br>**nephropathy?**<br>**If you are a carer (for someone with primary IgA**<br>**nephropathy) please share your experience of caring for**<br>**them**|My experience with IgA Nephropathy began in 2012, at the age of 24.<br>I had gained weight rapidly, putting on multiple kilograms within weeks, with pitting<br>oedema in my legs. It was when the oedema reached my abdomen that I sought medical<br>advice from my GP. A dip test confirmed significant levels of protein in my urine, and I was<br>referred Royal Berks hospital immediately.<br>Following a biopsy soon after, I was diagnosed with IgA Nephropathy, with an eGFR of<br>about 40. The initial treatment was a 6-month course of prednisolone to reduce the<br>inflammation, along with Ramipril to control blood pressure.<br>I’ll never forget the moment when the consultant told me that there were no specific<br>treatment for my condition, and that we would just need to manage the condition as best<br>we could. The pain of hearing that sentence will stay with me forever. End Stage Kidney<br>Disease was deemed likely, and it was estimated that it probably take about 10 years to<br>reach that point.<br>As someone who had recently finished university and was finding their feet in the world, it<br>came as a huge shock. The fact that I was working in the fitness industry and had always<br>deemed myself as being fit and healthy, made it even more overwhelming. Whilst the<br>physical symptoms were manageable at this stage, the emotional toll was immense.<br>Multiple rounds of psychological therapy and periods of medical intervention were required<br>to help me the mental challenge of living with a chronic disease at that age.<br>My kidney function remained relatively stable until around 2020 when it began to decline.<br>Slowly at first, but then more rapidly, and it was the start of 2022 when End Stage Kidney<br>Disease was deemed inevitable. The transplant process began. It was also around this<br>time when I was prescribed Dapagliflozin, but that didn’t seem to have too much impact.<br>I was fortunate enough to have a number of potential donors step forward for testing. Most<br>don’t have that privilege. The period was incredibly challenging due to the uncertainty<br>about my future. The emotional turmoil contributed to the breakdown of my marriage and<br>by the end of the year I had a mental breakdown. I was prescribed an SSRI for depression<br>and anxiety, and had more sessions with Talking Therapies.|
|||

It was from the end of 2022 into the beginning of 2023 that the physical symptoms of End Stage Kidney Disease reared their ugly head. I was constantly fatigued and completely drained. It literally felt like I was dragging myself around most of the time. My social life became non-existent as I didn’t have the energy to do much beyond exist, and I had to substantially reduce my working hours to the point were I needed financial help. 

Patient expert statement 

Sparsentan for treating primary IgA nephropathy [ID6308] 

6 of 10 



<!-- page 494 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

By late summer it was confirmed that my younger cousin was a suitable match, and the transplant was scheduled in Coventry for 13th October 2023. A difficult few months went by as my health continued to decline and anxiety increased, but the transplant went ahead successfully. What followed was an extremely intensive follow-up process with multiple trips to Oxford every week for a number of months. I was fortunate enough that my employer was supportive of this, but not everyone is so lucky. Just over a year later, the kidney continues to perform well and my eGFR has been stable throughout. However, I have had ongoing complications with neutropenia. It has been difficult feeling so much better, but still feeling restricted due to the immunosuppression. I’m fully aware that my battle with kidney disease is far from over, both mentally and psychically. A transplant is a treatment not a cure, and perhaps a treatment that could have been avoided with more sophisticated treatments.
